title: Understanding depression
subtitle: What is happening to me, and why it is not my fault
intro: Depression is one of the most common illnesses in the world, and one of the least understood by the people who have it. This first week lays the ground: what depression is and does, where it comes from, why it is nobody's fault, which myths keep people silent, and what getting help really looks like. Everything that follows builds on one fact: depression is treatable, and most people improve.

title: Thoughts and rumination
subtitle: Noticing the mind's habits and loosening their grip
intro: Depression does not only change how you feel; it changes how you think, and the thoughts then feed the feelings. This week looks at that loop: the automatic thoughts that arrive uninvited, the replay of rumination, the thinking traps that clinicians have named, and the practical skills of cognitive behavioural therapy for catching a thought, weighing it against the evidence, and answering it with something kinder and truer. It ends with one small action, because thinking and doing are not separate.

title: Movement
subtitle: The body as a doorway to the mind
intro: This week is about movement, in whatever size you can manage today. Researchers have compared walking programmes with antidepressants, measured how much movement matters, and followed people for months afterwards. The findings are more hopeful than most people expect, and the starting point is far smaller than you fear: a few minutes, a window, a street.

title: Sleep, light and rhythm
subtitle: Resetting the clock that depression disturbs
intro: This week is about sleep, light and the body clock. Poor sleep is one of the most common symptoms of depression, and the research shows it is also one of its causes, which makes it a place where small changes can matter. Over seven days we build a simple rhythm you can keep: a steady wake time, daylight in the morning, and a gentler end to the day.

title: Food and mood
subtitle: Feeding a brain that is working hard
intro: This week is about food and mood. Not a diet, not a list of forbidden things, and nothing that replaces your treatment. Your brain is built from what you eat and runs on it every hour, and research over the last fifteen years shows that the overall pattern of what we eat is linked to how we feel. We will look at what the studies really found, what they could not prove, and how to feed yourself in small, affordable ways on days when cooking feels impossible.

title: Water and small basics
subtitle: Simple things with measurable effects
intro: This week is about the smallest things that measurably move mood: water, regular food, morning light, one cleared surface. None of them treats depression on its own, and all of them go alongside your treatment, never in place of it. But depression quietly removes these basics first, and putting them back is something you can do on almost any day, even a bad one.

title: Outdoors
subtitle: Green, light and quiet for a restless mind
intro: This week is about going outside, or letting the outside in. Trees, daylight, birdsong and fresh air are not a treatment for depression on their own, but careful studies show they do something real to a tired, looping mind. Every challenge this week can be shrunk to five minutes by an open window.

title: What we reach for
subtitle: Alcohol, nicotine and the trap of quick relief
intro: Many of us reach for something when the day is too heavy: a drink, a cigarette, anything that works quickly. This week looks honestly, and without blame, at what alcohol and nicotine do to mood and sleep, why the relief backfires, and what the research says about the lift that follows stopping. It ends with a practical plan and a plain word about getting help safely.

title: Gratitude and strengths
subtitle: Training attention toward what is still good
intro: This week is about where your attention goes, and whether that can be trained. Depression pulls the mind towards what is missing, what went wrong and what might go wrong next. Researchers have tested small, concrete practices that pull it gently the other way: three good things, counting blessings, naming a strength, thanking a person. Some of them had effects that were still measurable six months later. None of them ask you to feel grateful on command, and we will be honest about where they can backfire.

title: Connection
subtitle: Why isolation feeds depression and how to step back in
intro: Depression pulls people away from each other at exactly the moment they need each other most. This week looks at what research says about connection: why withdrawing is a symptom rather than a failing, why belonging to groups protects against depression and relapse, and how the smallest step back towards people, one message or one shared room, counts. A faith community is one place to belong; choirs, classes, walking groups and support groups are others.

title: Trust and meaning
subtitle: Faith, hope and the long view
intro: This week is about trust and meaning. Believers get depressed too: Elijah, David, Jeremiah and Job all cried out, and the research shows that faith is often a real help in depression, though never a shield against it. Each day offers one honest, small step that works whether or not you believe, alongside any treatment you are receiving.

title: Getting help
subtitle: Therapy, medicine and building your care team
intro: This last week is about getting help, and about what the research honestly says help can do. We look at what a first appointment is like, what talking therapies and medication actually do, what happens when the first treatment does not work, and how to build a plan for the road ahead. None of it replaces what you have already practised; it adds to it.
